# FDG5114

> DO NOT pass reference types by reference (`ref` or `in`).

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 5.8.3 Parameter Passing.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG5114
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test none
- Status: draft

Message: Do not pass the reference type parameter '{0}' of '{1}' by reference

FDG5114 reports a ref, in or ref readonly parameter of a reference type (a class, interface, delegate, array or string, or a type parameter constrained to a reference type) of an externally visible method, constructor, delegate, operator or indexer. Overrides and interface implementations are not reported. The swap exception of the body is recognized by its shape: ref parameters are not reported when the member has two or more ref parameters of the same type. Other limited exceptions, such as a helper that assigns a caller's field through a ref parameter of a class-constrained type parameter (LazyInitializer.EnsureInitialized, Interlocked.Exchange, a property setter helper), are reported; such reports are false positives. in and ref readonly parameters are always reported, since the body says there is no reason for them. An unconstrained type parameter, as in the Swap<T> example, is not a reference type and is not reported. CA1045 is not mapped (see FDG5113). Changing how a public parameter is passed changes the public API, so the fix is breaking; there is no code fix.

## From the book

There are some limited exceptions to the rule, such as when a method can be used to swap references. There is no reason to pass a reference type with the `in` modifier (`ref readonly` semantics).

```csharp
public static class Reference {
  public void Swap<T>(ref T obj1, ref T obj2){
    T temp = obj1;
    obj1 = obj2;
    obj2 = temp;
  }
}
```

> **Chris Sells:** Swap always comes up in these discussions, but I have not written code that actually needed a swap function since college. Unless you’ve got a very good reason, avoid `out` and `ref` altogether.
